name: Archetype: Iron Age and classical infantry states

weightNotes.aggression: Seasonal raiding and invasion to force battle was the norm (Hanson for Greece; Italic and Celtic warfare such as the Allia 390s BC and Sentinum 295 BC); slightly above mid.
weightNotes.maneuver: Close-order or loose infantry lines meeting frontally; manoeuvre mostly at the wings. Attrition-leaning.
weightNotes.flanking: Cavalry or light troops on the wings sometimes turned a flank (Sentinum, Gallic and Samnite wings), but rarely as a designed plan; below mid.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Most such states lacked siege trains and took towns by blockade, storm or betrayal; open battle and ravaging preferred.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Single-line deployments were typical outside Rome's triplex acies; little reserve.
weightNotes.scouting: Small cavalry arms; ambushes and surprises are frequent in the record (Allia). Low.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Krentz (GRBS 1985): defeated classical armies typically lost 10-20% killed including pursuit, so the break came under 10%; Sabin (2000) finds the same pattern for Roman-era battles.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Infantry core with some cavalry, slingers and javelinmen, loosely coordinated; mid-low.
weightNotes.initiative: Citizen or tribal levies under a king, elected magistrate or chief; little drill below the top.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Short campaigns on rations and foraging near home; armies dispersed at harvest or when supplies ran out.

summary: Generic profile for Iron Age and classical states whose strength was infantry: Italic peoples, Celtic and Iberian tribes, smaller Greek and Hellenistic states and similar. Armies of citizen or tribal levies fought in a main infantry line with cavalry and skirmishers on the wings, in short summer campaigns of raiding and pitched battle. Battles were decided in hours by the collapse of one line, with most deaths in the pursuit.
whyItWorked: Cheap to raise from free farmers, effective at defending home territory, and able to field large numbers for a single decisive battle; heavy infantry was hard to stop frontally on level ground.
whereItFailed: Against professional, combined-arms or drilled enemies that could absorb shock and exploit flanks: Celtic and Samnite armies against Rome (Sentinum 295 BC), Greek states against Macedon (Chaeronea 338 BC), and against cavalry or horse-archer armies on open ground. Lack of siege craft and logistics prevented decisive wars of conquest.

sources.title: Krentz, Casualties in Hoplite Battles, GRBS 26 (1985)
Sabin, The Face of Roman Battle, JRS 90 (2000)
Hanson, The Western Way of War (2nd ed. 2000)
